keyVerseText: It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him.
rootMeaning: The root of גֵּוָה (gêvâh) is גֵּו (gêv), which broadly denotes the back or middle of something, often referring to the body. As the feminine form, גֵּוָה specifically means the back or the body itself, emphasizing the physical aspect of a person rather than a metaphorical or abstract sense. This root meaning enriches the English gloss "body" by highlighting the idea of the back as a central, structural part of the human form, suggesting strength and the hidden or internal aspect of the person.
usageInScripture: This word occurs only once in Scripture, appearing in Job 20:25, where it is translated as "body." The singular occurrence and consistent translation as a physical part of the person indicate that גֵּוָה is used concretely rather than figuratively. Its limited usage underscores its specificity, referring to the physical back or body from which something can emerge or be drawn out, as in the imagery of the verse.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גֵּוָה as the back or body enriches our grasp of biblical anthropology, reminding us that Scripture often speaks to the whole person, including the physical frame God created. The body is not merely a vessel but integral to the person’s identity and experience. In a Christian context, this highlights the incarnation of Christ, who took on full humanity, including a body with a back, emphasizing God's intimate involvement with the physical world. Moreover, the imagery of something coming out of the body can symbolize the reality of sin, judgment, or spiritual realities manifesting in tangible form, pointing to the holistic nature of salvation and judgment.
keyVerseReflection: Job 20:25 states, "It is drawn, and cometh out of the body; yea, the glittering sword cometh out of his gall: terrors are upon him." Here, גֵּוָה (body) grounds the vivid image of something being extracted from the very frame of a person, underscoring the reality of suffering and judgment that affects the whole being. The use of this word highlights the tangible and painful consequences of sin, making the spiritual realities profoundly physical and personal. This deepens the reader's understanding of the verse’s portrayal of divine retribution as something that touches the core of human existence.
